title: Hybrid Fetch Abstraction for Resumable Streams and Cross-Version Compatibility
creator: Asha Patel
description: Define and ship a cross-language "hybrid fetch" SDK abstraction that unifies paginated fetch, resumable streaming, and offline prefetch/backfill semantics for Python, TypeScript, and Go clients. This ticket clarifies requirements, scope, acceptance criteria, and the migration path for existing 'cursor' and 'stream' surfaces so production clients can gracefully upgrade without read or write interruptions.
background: Multiple customers and internal product teams need an SDK surface that supports: 1) long-lived streaming with ability to checkpoint and resume on disconnect, 2) paginated fetch for deterministic batch workloads, and 3) a hybrid mode where the client can switch between streaming and paginated fetching mid-session (for backfill or offline recovery). Current SDKs have ad-hoc patterns per language; we need a standardized abstraction and compatibility shims in the server and client to avoid divergence.
goals: Provide a single client-facing surface (hybridFetch) that supports streaming, paginated pulls, and resumable checkpoints
Ensure backwards-compatible upgrades for existing cursor + streaming clients without requiring server-side migration windows
Ship language idiomatic implementations for Python (async iterator), TypeScript (AsyncIterable/Node stream), and Go (channel + context) with matching semantics
Define clear retry and idempotency semantics for resumed sessions to avoid duplicated user-visible events
Document migration steps and provide small portability shims for common patterns
non_goals: Replacing existing long-running websocket-based-only integrations in one release
Guaranteeing exactly-once semantics for user-defined side effects (outside of idempotency headers)
Implementing custom persistence stores for checkpoints (clients will be responsible for checkpoint storage)
requirements: API: Add /v1/hybrid-fetch endpoint providing chunked responses with an optional stable resume_token header
Protocol: Server supplies 'Resume-Token' in response metadata periodically (configurable checkpoint interval) and accepts 'X-Resume-Token' on reconnect
Client: Python SDK exposes AsyncHybridIterator with methods next(), checkpoint(), resume(token), and close()
Client: TypeScript SDK returns an AsyncIterable plus an optional ReadableStream wrapper; exposes .checkpoint() and static .resumeFrom(token) factory
Client: Go SDK supports a typed Stream object that returns a channel of items and exposes Checkpoint() and Resume(ctx, token) methods
Retry semantics: Resume uses idempotency markers; the server must support replay from a resume token with at-most-once delivery of items already checkpointed by token
Compatibility: Server accepts both legacy 'cursor' header and new 'X-Resume-Token' header; when both present, prefer explicit 'X-Resume-Token' and log deprecation warnings
Backwards compatibility: Existing paginated endpoints must remain functional; new clients should be able to request page-based mode from the hybrid endpoint via ?mode=page
Performance: Hybrid mode must support HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming, HTTP/2, and gRPC transport with consistent resume tokens
Security: Resume tokens are short-lived opaque tokens produced server-side; SDKs must document and enforce secure storage recommendations (KMS/HSM for persisted tokens in enterprise docs)
acceptance_criteria: Python: Integration test demonstrating disconnect/reconnect where client checkpoints after 150 events and resumes using returned token; resulting stream contains no duplicates and completes to expected sequence
TypeScript: Node test using AsyncIterable wrapper that converts to Readable stream and successfully performs a mid-stream switch to 'page' mode to fetch historical 500 items without data loss
Go: Example application using context cancel then Resume(ctx, token) must resume within documented SLO (<= 200ms median for local tests) and honor context cancellation
Server: Adds Resume-Token metadata header and honors X-Resume-Token; logs deprecation warnings when legacy cursor used; pass internal conformance tests
API Compatibility: New SDK release does not require server forcing clients to upgrade; old clients continue to consume paginated and streaming endpoints with existing behavior
Docs: PRD + three language migration guides merged into docs repo and linked from SDK changelogs
Telemetry: Track resume success rate, median resume latency, and any duplicate item counts for first 30 days post-launch; dashboards created in console-telemetry project
migration_strategy: Phased rollout: 1) Server protocol layer declares support and emits Resume-Token for hybrid-capable endpoints (no client changes required). 2) Ship client SDK support behind feature flag; provide opt-in migration shims. 3) After 60 days and telemetry review, enable opt-out grace period with deprecation notices to customers using legacy cursors. 4) Publish best-practice snippets for checkpoint storage and token lifetime handling.
rollout_plan: Week 0: API spec reviewed and approved by eng + security
Week 1: Server-side resume token support implemented behind feature flag; internal conformance tests added
Week 2-3: Language SDK implementations and integration tests
Week 4: Docs + migration guide + sample apps; feature flag enabled in staging
Week 5: Canary release to 5 pilot customers; monitor metrics
Week 7: Gradual ramp to GA if resume success >= 99.5% and duplicate rate < 0.01%
testing_notes: Create fault-injection harness that simulates mid-stream TCP drop and reconnect with randomized delay (50ms-10s)
Verify at-least/at-most semantics by instrumenting item IDs and checkpoint offsets in integration tests
End-to-end tests for HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2, and gRPC transports
Language-savvy unit tests to validate iterator/stream ergonomics and TypeScript type definitions
implementation_notes: Server: Maintain deterministic sequence numbering per stream session to allow resume token to encode offset and session checksum
Server: Resume tokens are HMAC-signed + timestamped to prevent tampering; rotation managed via KMS
SDK: Expose explicit 'checkpointInterval' config with a sane default (100 items or 30s) and allow override
SDK: Provide a small 'resume-persistence' helper package for each language (optional) demonstrating local encrypted storage patterns
SDK: Keep legacy 'cursor' helpers but prefer deprecation-safe wrappers that emit telemetry when used
tradeoffs: Exact-once side-effects are not guaranteed: we limit scope to at-most-once semantically for items acknowledged by resume tokens; callers with external side effects must still implement idempotency
Adding resume tokens increases response metadata size; we checkpoint periodically to avoid per-item metadata overhead
Server complexity rises to support replay and sequence checksums; trade for better client uptime and simpler client logic
open_questions: Should resume tokens be revocable by admin via console? (security vs convenience)
What default TTL is appropriate for tokens for enterprise compliance (15m vs 24h)?
Do we need to surface a 'resumed_from_version' field so clients can detect server-side model/schema changes that would require a forced re-fetch?
notes: This ticket ties to broader SDK convergence effort. Engineering should collaborate early with Security on token format and with DX on ergonomics. If telemetry shows high dup rates in canary, pause rollout and investigate server-side checkpointing frequency.
